newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ pension scheme would lower funding costs-Peters.
newsitem.headline: NZ pension scheme would lower funding costs-Peters.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters said on Thursday savers would not be penalised under a proposed compulsory pension scheme and that the scheme would result in lower borrowing costs.
"Existing savers will not be disadvantaged," Peters said in a speech to the Auckland Business Network.
"One of the guidelines for the detailed design is that people who have had the foresight to save will not be penalised," he said.
The scheme would either have minimal or no costs to business. Payments would accompany the pay-as-you-earn tax system to ensure low compliance costs.
"Another positive for the business community, and the nation at large, is that increased savings of the magnitude expected under the scheme will lower the costs of borrowing," he said.
Peters said there was some evidence that New Zealanders were saving more voluntarily.
But the question remained as to whether that was enough to cope with demographic changes, or whether those savings would be used to provide a retirement income.
Too much was being made of home ownership as a form of saving for retirement, he said.
"It is far better to spread one's risk -- house prices can just as easily fall, taking a homeowner's net worth down with it," he said.

Women and other groups who could not earn enough to save for their retirement would be looked after by the government and the state would continue to ensure that the elderly had sufficient income in retirement.
"We are not claiming that any scheme can suddenly make it possible for all people, women and men to save enough for retirement.
"The Government will continue to play its role to make sure the elderly are supported," he said.
On Monday Peters told a Wellington audience the scheme, still being drawn up, would not be guaranteed and that on retirement, people were likely to be able to take only an annuity, not a lump sum.
Peters suggested the annuity should total NZ$160,000 per person, but he said today the sum was merely indicative.
"However, people shouldn't be unrealistic about the level of savings needed to provide a reasonable annuity. The real message from this is that we want people to save."
The scheme was not another tax, as had been suggested.

"How is it a tax if the money stays in your account and will contribute to your income in retirement? As you know we are able to make a tax cut next year, and we aim to make further cuts in later years, as the economy permits."
The superannuation issue is to go before a national referendum in September.
